docs.title: 6. The optimisation process
docs.text: This chapter follows one mission through the program, from the case file to the verified optimum: what each stage computes, what it passes to the next one, and why the stages are arranged this way. The equations behind each step are in chapter 7, and the solver itself in chapter 8.

docs.title: 6.1 Why the optimisation is staged
docs.text:
Trajectory optimisation is solved here as a large nonlinear program (NLP): thousands of variables and constraints, a nonconvex feasible set (no-fly zones, nonlinear dynamics) and a cost with several local minima. IPOPT, like every gradient-based solver, converges to a local optimum near its initial point, and how quickly and reliably it does so depends heavily on that point.

Two facts follow:

  1. A good initial point matters more than any solver option. A straight line from start to goal violates the equations of motion (it has zero controls), may cross the no-fly zones, and ignores the final heading. IPOPT must first repair all of this, and may end in a poor local optimum or fail. The thesis measured exactly this: without a warm start, the point-mass problem was infeasible in 3 of its 8 scenarios (14. Warm-start benchmark). Exercise 2 of the tutorial shows a milder version with the generic UAV: a cold start ends 25 % slower and 20 % heavier on fuel in mission T-03.
  2. A cheap model can prepare an expensive one. The point-mass model has 8 states and an analytic Jacobian; the 6-DoF model has 13 states and a numerical one. Solving the point-mass problem first, and projecting its optimum into 6-DoF states, gives the expensive problem a starting point that is already close to optimal.

The pipeline therefore increases the fidelity in steps: a geometric path, a flown trajectory, a point-mass optimum and finally a 6-DoF optimum, each serving as the initial point of the next.

docs.title: 6.2 Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Case file: aircraft, mission, pipeline settings"] --> R["Mission references<br/>L_ref, t_ref, scales, t_f bounds"]
    A --> W1
    subgraph WS ["1. Warm start (ws::build)"]
        W1["Hybrid A* path<br/>around the active zones, through the waypoints"] --> W2["Guidance laws fly the path<br/>UF: dynamic inversion; FC: autopilot"]
    end
    W2 -->|"UF run, resampled on N_uf nodes"| U
    R --> U
    subgraph UF ["2. Point-mass stage"]
        U["ocp::UfProblem<br/>1 + 11 N variables"] --> U2["IPOPT"] --> U3["nlp::verify"]
    end
    U3 -->|"UF optimum, resampled on N_fc nodes"| P["3. Projection ws::ufToFc<br/>attitude, rates, surfaces"]
    P --> F
    R --> F
    subgraph FC ["4. Rigid-body stage"]
        F["ocp::FcProblem<br/>1 + 17 N variables"] --> F2["IPOPT"] --> F3["nlp::verify"]
    end
    F3 --> O["5. Post-checks and export<br/>clearance, waypoint miss, simulation error, CSV, JSON"]

The whole sequence is pipeline::run in src/pipeline/pipeline.cpp. It returns a pipeline::Result with the warm start, the initial point and the optimum of each stage, and a Stage record (status, iterations, time, objective, verification) for each of them.

docs.title: 6.3 Before the stages: the mission references
docs.text:
Before anything is solved, the pipeline fixes the quantities that define the size of the problem, all computed from the mission and never from an initial point:

  • the reference length \(L_{ref}\): the polyline start → waypoints → goal, combined with the altitude change;
  • the reference time \(t_{ref} = L_{ref}/V\), with \(V\) the commanded speed V_mps.

They set the scales of the position variables and of the flight time, the bounds of the flight time (\(0.3\,t_{ref} \le t_f \le 3\,t_{ref}\)) and the normalisation of the cost (chapter 7). Because they do not depend on the seed, a cold start, a warm start and a projected optimum all solve the same problem, and their results can be compared directly (UC-09). The only exception is the assignment of waypoints to nodes, which follows the initial point (section 6.5).

docs.title: 6.4 Stage 1: warm start
docs.text:
ws::build in src/warmstart/warm_start.cpp produces a trajectory that is flyable, avoids the zones and visits the waypoints. It is not optimal, and it is not meant to be.

  1. Turn radius. \(R = V^2/(g\tan(f_b\,\phi_{ws}))\) from the commanded speed, the warm-start bank bank_deg and bank_fraction \(f_b\). For the bundled missions: 25 m/s, 30° and 0.8 give 143 m.
  2. Path planning. Hybrid A* searches over cells of position and heading. Its edges are short arcs and straight segments whose curvature never exceeds \(1/R\), so every path it returns can be flown at the planning bank. Points along each edge must keep margin_m + safety_m from every active zone. A Dubins path (the shortest path with bounded curvature between two poses) serves as heuristic and, when it is collision-free, closes the search early. With waypoints, the mission is planned leg by leg. Details: Formulation in code, missions with no-fly zones.
  3. Flying the path. The path is a geometric curve without speeds or timing. Guidance laws fly it with both models, by RK4 integration at 100 Hz:
    • lateral: L1 path following, which aims at a point 2.5 V ahead on the path and commands the bank needed to reach it;
    • vertical: a climb or descent at up to gamma_deg towards the final altitude;
    • point mass: the equations of motion are inverted for lift coefficient, thrust and bank rate (dynamic inversion);
    • rigid body: an autopilot around the wings-level trim drives elevator, aileron, rudder and thrust.
  4. Resampling. The UF run is interpolated in time onto the \(N_{uf}\) collocation nodes (ws::fromRun).

The flown trajectories satisfy the equations of motion of their model, so their collocation defects are small; they are only nonzero because the mesh is coarser than the integration step. In the tutorial, the warm start's largest normalised defect is 0.22–0.29, against 3.2 for a straight line (guess_defect_uf in summary.csv).

The warm start succeeds if a path is found and the point-mass guidance reaches its end. If it fails, the row is marked (CHECK) and the UF stage starts from a straight line instead.

docs.title: 6.5 Stage 2: the point-mass problem
docs.text:
1. Initial point. The resampled UF run (seed label warm start (UF guidance run)), or with "seed": "cold" a straight line at constant speed with zero controls (straight line).
  2. Mission data. Start state (position, V_mps, level, start_heading_deg, wings level, take-off mass), goal position, altitude and heading, cost weights.
  3. No-fly zones. The margin of every zone is enlarged so that the straight segments between nodes, not only the nodes, keep the requested margin (section 7.5).
  4. Waypoints. Each waypoint is attached to one node: the node of the initial point nearest to it, searching forward from the previous waypoint's node and leaving room for the remaining waypoints. The waypoint constraint then applies to that node.
  5. Problem. ocp::UfProblem assembles the variables, bounds, constraints, sparse Jacobian and cost (chapter 7).
  6. Solve. nlp::solve calls IPOPT (chapter 8).
  7. Verify. nlp::verify re-evaluates every constraint and bound at the result (section 4.3). The stage succeeds only if IPOPT converged and the verification passed.
  8. Penalty share. The cost is re-evaluated with the smoothness weights set to zero; the difference is reported as pen%.

Because waypoints are attached to fixed nodes, the share of the flight time before each waypoint follows the initial point. With a good warm start this costs little; with a poor initial point it can steer the solver towards a worse optimum, which is one reason the cold start of tutorial mission T-03 ends worse.

docs.title: 6.6 Stage 3: projection from point mass to rigid body
docs.text:
ws::ufToFc turns the point-mass optimum, resampled on \(N_{fc}\) nodes, into 6-DoF states and controls, node by node:

  1. The incidence follows from the lift coefficient, and the elevator from the pitching-moment balance. Since the 6-DoF thrust acts along the body axis rather than the velocity, it is \(T/\cos\alpha\); three fixed-point passes settle incidence, elevator and thrust together.
  2. The attitude is the wind-axis attitude (flight-path angle, heading, bank) rotated by the incidence, with zero sideslip. Roll, pitch and yaw angles are extracted from the resulting rotation matrix.
  3. Body rates are obtained from the time derivatives of the Euler angles.
  4. Body velocities are \((V\cos\alpha, 0, V\sin\alpha)\).
  5. Aileron and rudder cancel the rolling and yawing moments at zero sideslip.

On a trimmed straight line, the projection reproduces the 6-DoF trim to five digits. On a manoeuvring trajectory its defects are larger (2.7–4.9 in the tutorial), because the point mass has no rotational dynamics, but the trajectory is already close to the 6-DoF optimum in position, speed and timing.

docs.title: 6.7 Stage 4: the rigid-body problem
docs.text:
The FC stage is seeded by the first available option:

Condition Initial point Seed label in report.json fc_from_uf is true and the UF stage succeeded The projected UF optimum UF optimum (projected) Otherwise, the warm start succeeded and the FC autopilot reached the goal The FC run of the warm start, resampled warm start (FC autopilot run) Otherwise, the warm start succeeded The UF run of the warm start, projected warm start (UF guidance run, projected) Otherwise (cold start) A straight line with every node at the wings-level trim straight line (trimmed)

The initial state is the 6-DoF wings-level trim at V_mps and h0_m, placed at the start position and heading. The end conditions, zones, waypoints and cost weights are those of the UF stage, plus the sideslip limit sideslip_max_deg. The problem is ocp::FcProblem; it is solved and verified in the same way as the UF stage.

docs.title: 6.8 Post-checks
docs.text:
The constraints of the NLP hold at the nodes. After the solve, the pipeline measures the optimum more finely:

Check How Reported as Zone clearance Distance beyond the margin of every active zone, at ten points per segment between nodes clrUF, clrFC Waypoint miss Smallest distance from each waypoint to the path, at eleven points per segment wpUF, wpFC Discretisation error (UF) Each interval simulated with RK4 (step ≤ 0.01 s) from its starting node, with the optimal controls interpolated linearly; distance to the next node simUF

docs.title: 6.9 Inside one solve
docs.text:
Each IPOPT call repeats the same loop until its convergence test is met (details in chapter 8):

  1. Evaluate the cost, its gradient, the constraints and their sparse Jacobian at the current point. These are the only things the formulation provides; IPOPT never sees the aircraft, only these numbers.
  2. Update a limited-memory approximation of the second derivatives from the last few gradient changes.
  3. Solve one sparse linear system (the Newton step of the barrier problem) for a search direction.
  4. Choose a step length along that direction that reduces either the cost or the constraint violation (filter line search).
  5. Reduce the barrier parameter when the current barrier problem is solved accurately enough.

The IPOPT log of the UF stage of mission M-01 shows the typical course of a warm-started solve:

  • In the first ten iterations the barrier parameter stays at about 0.5, and IPOPT reduces the largest constraint violation from 0.3 to 0.004, accepting a higher cost on the way (0.46 to 1.56).
  • The adaptive barrier update then lowers \(\mu\) quickly, though not monotonically, to its floor of \(10^{-11}\) by iteration 42, while the cost falls to 0.390.
  • The remaining iterations refine the solution: the cost changes only in its fourth digit, and the solve stops at iteration 100 with a constraint violation of \(4\cdot10^{-9}\) and a dual infeasibility of \(9\cdot10^{-7}\), both below the tolerance of \(10^{-6}\).

Chapter 8 reproduces this log and explains each column.

docs.title: 6.10 Choosing the pipeline settings
docs.text:
Decision Recommendation Seed Always warm. cold is only useful to measure the value of the warm start Stages UF for route studies, quick trade-offs and many missions. UF>FC when attitudes, body rates or control-surface deflections matter, or to confirm the point-mass result with the full model Nodes Enough to resolve the turns. For the bundled 3–4 km missions, 60 nodes (one every 50–70 m) keep simUF under 1 m. Check simUF and refine if it is large compared with your accuracy needs. The cost of one iteration grows roughly linearly with N alpha 1 for minimum fuel, 0 for minimum time; intermediate values trade one against the other (tutorial, section 5.7) beta_control, beta_state Keep 1 unless pen% exceeds a few percent. Values near 0 give bang-bang thrust and saw-tooth altitude profiles in minimum-fuel problems sideslip_max_deg Keep 1°. It enforces coordinated flight, which the linear aerodynamic model needs to give physically meaningful 6-DoF optima Solver options The defaults suit these problems. Chapter 8 lists when to change them

For a fair comparison of seeds or stage sequences on your own missions, use UC-09 with the pipelines you want to compare (section 3.5).

docs.title: 7. Mathematical formulation
docs.text: This chapter states the complete optimisation problem that the public code solves: the models, every constraint, the bounds, the cost, the discretisation and the scaling. Each section names the source file that implements it. The thesis chapters 5 to 10 give the theory and the production formulation; this chapter describes the code in code/, which differs from the production solver in a few places (section 7.11).

docs.title: 7.1 The optimal-control problem
docs.text:
Find the flight time \(t_f\), the state history \(x(t)\) and the control history \(u(t)\) that solve

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{t_f,\;x(\cdot),\;u(\cdot)}\quad & J = (1-\alpha)\,\frac{t_f}{t_{ref}} + \alpha\,\frac{\text{fuel}(t_f)}{\text{fuel}_{ref}} + J_{smooth}\\[4pt] \text{subject to}\quad & \dot x(t) = f\big(x(t),u(t)\big), && 0 \le t \le t_f\\ & x(0) = x_{start}\\ & \psi_f\big(x(t_f)\big) = 0 && \text{final position and heading}\\ & h\big(x(t),u(t)\big) \le 0 && \text{envelope and no-fly zones}\\ & \lVert p(t_w) - p_w\rVert \le r_w && \text{each waypoint } w\\ & x_{lo}\le x(t)\le x_{hi},\quad u_{lo}\le u(t)\le u_{hi},\quad t_{f,lo}\le t_f\le t_{f,hi} \end{aligned} \]

where \(f\) is the point-mass model (UF, section 7.3) or the rigid-body model (FC, section 7.4), \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) weighs time against fuel, and \(J_{smooth}\) penalises control and attitude increments between nodes. The problem is transcribed into a finite-dimensional nonlinear program (NLP) by trapezoidal collocation (section 7.8) and solved with IPOPT (chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.2 Atmosphere, aerodynamics and propulsion
docs.text:
Implemented in atmosphere.cpp and aircraft.cpp.

Atmosphere. International Standard Atmosphere, troposphere, valid from -500 m to 11 km (altitudes outside are clamped):

\[ T = T_0 - \lambda h,\qquad p = p_0\left(\frac{T}{T_0}\right)^{g_0/(R\lambda)},\qquad \rho = \frac{p}{RT},\qquad \sigma=\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \]

with \(T_0 = 288.15\) K, \(p_0 = 101325\) Pa, \(\lambda = 0.0065\) K/m, \(R = 287.053\) J/(kg K), \(g_0 = 9.80665\) m/s².

Aerodynamics. With the dynamic pressure \(\bar q = \tfrac12\rho V^2\) and the wing area \(S\), lift and drag are \(L=\bar q S C_L\) and \(D=\bar q S C_D\), with the parabolic polar

\[ C_D = C_{D0} + k\,C_L^2 . \]

The maximum lift coefficient and the stall speed are derived from the aircraft data:

\[ C_{L,max} = C_{L0} + C_{L\alpha}\,\alpha_{max},\qquad V_{stall}(h,m) = \sqrt{\frac{2mg_0}{\rho(h)\,S\,C_{L,max}}} . \]

Propulsion. A propeller driven by a naturally aspirated engine whose shaft power lapses with density (Gagg–Ferrar):

\[ P_{max}(h) = P_{max,0}\,\max\big(0,\;1.132\,\sigma - 0.132\big),\qquad T_{max}(V,h) = \frac{\eta_p\,P_{max}(h)}{\max\big(V,\,V_{stall}(h,m_0)\big)} . \]

Fuel flow. The specific fuel consumption \(\text{sfc}\) (kg/kWh) refers to shaft power, and the shaft power is the thrust power divided by the propeller efficiency:

\[ \dot m = -c\,T\,V,\qquad c = \frac{\text{sfc}}{3.6\times10^{6}\,\eta_p}\quad[\text{kg/J}]. \]

docs.title: 7.3 Point-mass model (UF)
docs.text:
Implemented in point_mass.cpp (uf::rhs, and the analytic Jacobian uf::jacobian).

State Symbol Unit Control Symbol Unit North position \(x_N\) m Thrust \(T\) N East position \(y_E\) m Lift coefficient \(C_L\) – Down position (\(-h\)) \(z_D\) m Bank rate \(p_\mu\) rad/s Airspeed \(V\) m/s Flight-path angle \(\gamma\) rad Heading \(\chi\) rad Bank angle \(\mu\) rad Mass \(m\) kg \[ \begin{aligned} \dot x_N &= V\cos\gamma\cos\chi, & \dot y_E &= V\cos\gamma\sin\chi, & \dot z_D &= -V\sin\gamma,\\ \dot V &= \frac{T-D}{m} - g_0\sin\gamma, & \dot\gamma &= \frac{L\cos\mu}{mV} - \frac{g_0\cos\gamma}{V}, & \dot\chi &= \frac{L\sin\mu}{mV\cos\gamma},\\ \dot\mu &= p_\mu, & \dot m &= -c\,T\,V . \end{aligned} \]

The thrust acts along the velocity, and the lift coefficient is a control: the incidence dynamics are much faster than the trajectory, so the aircraft is assumed to reach any lift coefficient instantly. The bank angle is a state, driven by the bank rate, so that bank changes take time. The load factor is \(n = L/(mg_0)\). The model supports a constant wind (added to the position rates), which is zero in UC-08 and UC-09.

uf::jacobian returns \(A=\partial f/\partial x\) and \(B=\partial f/\partial u\) in closed form, including the altitude dependence of the density, \(\partial\rho/\partial h = \rho\,(g_0/(R\lambda)-1)\,(-\lambda/T)\).

docs.title: 7.4 Rigid-body model (FC)
docs.text:
Implemented in rigid_body.cpp (fc::rhs).

State Symbol Unit Control Symbol Unit Position (NED) \(x_N, y_E, z_D\) m Thrust \(T\) N Body velocity \(u, v, w\) m/s Elevator \(\delta_e\) rad Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw) \(\phi, \theta, \psi\) rad Aileron \(\delta_a\) rad Body rates \(p, q, r\) rad/s Rudder \(\delta_r\) rad Mass \(m\) kg

Each evaluation proceeds in five steps.

1. Air data. With \(R_{nb}(\phi,\theta,\psi)\) the body-to-NED rotation (3-2-1 Euler sequence) and \(\mathbf w\) the wind in NED axes, the air-relative velocity in body axes is \(\mathbf v_r = (u,v,w)^\top - R_{nb}^\top\mathbf w\), and

\[ V_a = \lVert\mathbf v_r\rVert,\qquad \alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(w_r,\,u_r),\qquad \beta = \arcsin(v_r/V_a). \]

2. Aerodynamic coefficients. Linear stability derivatives, with non-dimensional rates \(\hat p = pb/(2V_a)\), \(\hat q = q\bar c/(2V_a)\), \(\hat r = rb/(2V_a)\):

\[ \begin{aligned} C_L &= C_{L0} + C_{L\alpha}\alpha + C_{Lq}\hat q + C_{L\delta_e}\delta_e, & C_D &= C_{D0} + k\,C_L^2,\\ C_Y &= C_{Y0} + C_{Y\beta}\beta + C_{Yp}\hat p + C_{Yr}\hat r + C_{Y\delta_a}\delta_a + C_{Y\delta_r}\delta_r,\\ C_l &= C_{l0} + C_{l\beta}\beta + C_{lp}\hat p + C_{lr}\hat r + C_{l\delta_a}\delta_a + C_{l\delta_r}\delta_r,\\ C_m &= C_{m0} + C_{m\alpha}\alpha + C_{mq}\hat q + C_{m\delta_e}\delta_e,\\ C_n &= C_{n0} + C_{n\beta}\beta + C_{np}\hat p + C_{nr}\hat r + C_{n\delta_a}\delta_a + C_{n\delta_r}\delta_r . \end{aligned} \]

3. Forces. The wind-axis forces \((-D,\,Y,\,-L)\), with \(D=\bar qSC_D\), \(Y=\bar qSC_Y\), \(L=\bar qSC_L\), are rotated to body axes by \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Weight and thrust (along the body \(x\) axis) are added:

\[ \mathbf F = R_{bw}(\alpha,\beta)\begin{pmatrix}-D\\Y\\-L\end{pmatrix} + m g_0\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\theta\\ \sin\phi\cos\theta\\ \cos\phi\cos\theta\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}T\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}. \]

4. Moments. Aerodynamic moments plus the pitching moment of a thrust line offset \(z_T\) below the centre of gravity:

\[ \mathbf M = \big(\bar qSb\,C_l,\;\; \bar qS\bar c\,C_m + z_T T,\;\; \bar qSb\,C_n\big)^\top . \]

5. Equations of motion.

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{\mathbf v}_b &= \frac{\mathbf F}{m} - \boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_b, & I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega} &= \mathbf M - \boldsymbol\omega\times I\boldsymbol\omega,\\ \dot{\mathbf r}_{NED} &= R_{nb}\,\mathbf v_b, & \dot m &= -c\,T\,V_a, \end{aligned} \] \[ \dot\phi = p + \tan\theta\,(q\sin\phi + r\cos\phi),\qquad \dot\theta = q\cos\phi - r\sin\phi,\qquad \dot\psi = \frac{q\sin\phi + r\cos\phi}{\cos\theta}, \]

with the inertia tensor \(I\) including the product \(I_{xz}\), inverted in closed form. The Euler kinematics are singular at \(\theta=\pm90°\); the pitch bound of section 7.6 keeps the solver away from it.

The FC Jacobian is computed by central differences of fc::rhs, with a step proportional to each variable's scale. Its structural sparsity is detected once, at a generic point, and only those entries are passed to the solver.

docs.title: Coordinated flight and the sideslip limit
docs.text: The parabolic polar has no drag due to sideslip. Without a limit on \(\beta\), the minimum-fuel 6-DoF optimum exploits this: it flies 15–27° sideways with the rudder saturated, so that the side force \(C_{Y\beta}\beta\) carries part of the weight at no drag cost, and appears to burn 6–9 % less fuel than the point mass, which is physically impossible for the same aircraft. The FC problem therefore includes the path constraint \(\beta^2/\beta_{max}^2-1\le0\), with \(\beta_{max}\) = sideslip_max_deg (1° by default). With it, the UF and FC optima agree to 0.2 % in fuel.

docs.title: 7.5 Path constraints
docs.text: Path constraints are evaluated at every node \(k\) and written as \(h(x_k,u_k)\le0\). Each row is normalised by its limit, so that a value of 0.01 means "1 % beyond the limit" whatever the physical quantity. The rows are built in TrapezoidalUF::pathAt (transcription.cpp) and FcProblem::pathAt (ocp_fc.cpp).

docs.title: Point mass: 12 rows per node, plus one per zone

Two-sided symmetric limits (bank, rates, sideslip) are written as one smooth quadratic row instead of two linear ones.

docs.title: No-fly zones
docs.text:
For zone \(j\) with polygon \(\mathcal P_j\) and margin \(m_j\), let \(d_j(x,y)\) be the signed distance from the point to the polygon: the distance to the nearest edge, positive outside and negative inside (crossing-number test). The row is

\[ h_{nfz,j} = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\tilde m_j - d_j(x_k,y_k)}{\max(\tilde m_j,\,25\ \text{m})} & \text{if zone } j \text{ is active}\\[8pt] -1 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]

A zone is active if its altitude band \([h_{min,j},h_{max,j}]\) overlaps the mission's band \([\min(h_0,h_f),\max(h_0,h_f)]\). The decision is made once per mission: a row that switched on and off with the node's altitude would be discontinuous, which a gradient-based solver cannot handle. Inactive zones keep a constant row so that the problem size does not depend on the mission's altitudes.

Margin between nodes. The rows hold at the nodes only, and the trajectory between two nodes is (to first order) a straight chord. If both ends of a chord of length \(\ell\) keep a distance \(\tilde m\) from a polygon corner, every point of the chord keeps at least \(\sqrt{\tilde m^2 - \ell^2/4}\). The pipeline therefore enforces at the nodes the inflated margin

\[ \tilde m_j = \sqrt{m_j^2 + \left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2},\qquad \ell = \frac{1.5\,L_{ref}}{N-1}, \]

where \(\ell\) is the node spacing of a path 50 % longer than the reference length (to allow for detours). Where the nearest feature is a straight edge rather than a corner, the distance varies linearly along the chord, so its minimum is at an end and the bound holds as well. For mission M-01 (\(L_{ref}\) = 3000 m, \(N\) = 60, \(m\) = 40 m): \(\ell\) = 76 m and \(\tilde m\) = 55 m. The post-check of section 6.8 confirms the real margin along the whole path.

docs.title: 7.7 Cost function
docs.text:
Implemented in TrapezoidalUF::cost and FcProblem::cost, with analytic gradients (costGradient) checked against finite differences by the tests.

Point mass.

\[ J_{UF} = (1-\alpha)\,\frac{t_f}{t_{ref}} + \alpha\,\frac{E}{E_{ref}} + \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\left[\beta_c\sum_{j\in\{T,\,C_L,\,p_\mu\}}\left(\frac{u_{j,k+1}-u_{j,k}}{s_{u_j}}\right)^{2} + \beta_s\sum_{i\in\{\gamma,\,\mu\}}\left(\frac{x_{i,k+1}-x_{i,k}}{s_{x_i}}\right)^{2}\right] \]

with the propulsive energy (thrust work) integrated by the trapezoidal rule,

\[ E = \sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\bar T_k\,\bar V_k\,\Delta t,\qquad \bar T_k = \tfrac12(T_k+T_{k+1}),\quad \bar V_k = \tfrac12(V_k+V_{k+1}). \]

Since the fuel burnt is \(cE\), minimising \(E\) minimises fuel.

Rigid body.

\[ J_{FC} = (1-\alpha)\,\frac{t_f}{t_{ref}} + \alpha\,\frac{m_0-m_{N-1}}{m_{ref}} + \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\left[\beta_c\sum_{j\in\{T,\,\delta_e,\,\delta_a,\,\delta_r\}}\left(\frac{\Delta u_{j,k}}{s_{u_j}}\right)^{2} + \beta_s\sum_{i\in\{\phi,\,\theta\}}\left(\frac{\Delta x_{i,k}}{s_{x_i}}\right)^{2}\right] \]

Here the fuel is read directly from the mass state, which integrates \(\dot m=-cTV_a\).

References. \(t_{ref} = \max(L_{ref}/V,\,1\ \text{s})\), \(E_{ref} = T_{ref}\,V_{cruise}\,t_{ref}\) and \(m_{ref} = c\,E_{ref}\), with \(T_{ref} = T_{max}(V_{cruise},0)\). Because \(m_{ref}=cE_{ref}\), the fuel terms of \(J_{UF}\) and \(J_{FC}\) are equal for the same flight, and the two costs are on the same scale. The references depend on the mission only, so they are the same for every seed.

The weights.

  • \(\alpha\) moves the optimum between minimum time (\(\alpha=0\)) and minimum fuel (\(\alpha=1\)). Both terms are of order one, so intermediate values give a genuine trade-off (tutorial, section 5.7).
  • \(\beta_c\) and \(\beta_s\) penalise node-to-node changes of the controls and of the attitude-like states. Without them a minimum-fuel optimum is bang-bang: thrust jumps between zero and its maximum, and the aircraft follows a saw-tooth of glides and climbs. With \(\beta_c=\beta_s=1\) the penalty is 0–1 % of the final cost in the bundled missions. The division by \(N-1\) makes the penalty of node-to-node oscillations independent of the number of nodes, while the penalty of a smooth trajectory vanishes as the mesh is refined. The thesis discusses this regularisation in 10. Cost function and 13. Regularisation.

docs.title: 7.8 Transcription by trapezoidal collocation
docs.text:
Implemented in collocation.cpp (trapezoidalDefects, trapezoidalJacobian).

The time interval is divided into \(N-1\) equal intervals of length \(\Delta t = t_f/(N-1)\). States and controls are decision variables at every node, and the dynamics are imposed on each interval by the trapezoidal rule. The defect of interval \(k\) is

\[ \boldsymbol\Delta_k = \operatorname{diag}(s_x)^{-1}\left[x_{k+1} - x_k - \frac{\Delta t}{2}\Big(f(x_k,u_k) + f(x_{k+1},u_{k+1})\Big)\right] = 0,\qquad k = 0,\dots,N-2 . \]

The scaling by the state scales \(s_x\) makes every defect row dimensionless and comparable. The local truncation error of the trapezoidal rule is \(O(\Delta t^3)\) and the global error \(O(\Delta t^2)\); a test checks the \(\Delta t^3\) decay on a smooth reference trajectory. Because \(t_f\) is a variable, \(\Delta t\) is too, and every defect depends on \(t_f\).

The Jacobian of interval \(k\), with \(A_k=\partial f/\partial x\) and \(B_k=\partial f/\partial u\) at node \(k\), has the blocks (before row scaling):

With respect to Block \(x_k\) \(-I - \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}A_k\) \(x_{k+1}\) \(I - \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}A_{k+1}\) \(u_k\) \(-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}B_k\) \(u_{k+1}\) \(-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}B_{k+1}\) \(t_f\) \(-\tfrac{1}{2(N-1)}\big(f_k + f_{k+1}\big)\)

Each interval couples only two neighbouring nodes, so the defect Jacobian is block-banded and very sparse: at \(N=200\), only 0.44 % of the UF defect Jacobian's entries are nonzero (UC-04).

docs.title: 7.9 The resulting NLP
docs.text:
The decision vector stacks the flight time, the states and the controls:

\[ z = \big[\,t_f \;\big|\; x_0,\,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1} \;\big|\; u_0,\,u_1,\dots,u_{N-1}\,\big] . \]

The constraint vector \(g(z)\) has four blocks, in this order:

Block Rows Bounds Content Defects \((N-1)\,n_x\) \(= 0\) Section 7.8 Boundary \(n_x + 4\) \(= 0\) Section 7.6 Path \(N\,(n_c + n_z)\) \(\le 0\) Section 7.5, node by node Waypoints \(n_w\) \(\le 0\) Section 7.6

with \(n_x\) states, \(n_u\) controls, \(n_c\) envelope rows, \(n_z\) zones and \(n_w\) waypoints.

UF FC \(n_x\), \(n_u\), \(n_c\) 8, 3, 12 13, 4, 16 Variables \(1 + 11N\) \(1 + 17N\) Equality constraints \(8(N-1) + 12\) \(13(N-1) + 17\) Inequality constraints \((12 + n_z)N + n_w\) \((16 + n_z)N + n_w\) Example: \(N = 60\), one zone, no waypoint 661 variables, 484 equalities, 780 inequalities 1021 variables, 784 equalities, 1020 inequalities

The UF numbers are those IPOPT prints for mission M-01 (section 8.4).

Jacobian. CollocationProblem::constraintJacobian (ocp_problem.cpp) returns the nonzero entries as (row, column, value) triplets, always in the same order:

  • defect rows: the blocks of section 7.8, from the analytic UF Jacobian or the central-difference FC Jacobian, keeping only structurally nonzero entries;
  • boundary rows: one constant entry each;
  • path rows: the rows of node \(k\) depend only on \((x_k,u_k)\), so each node contributes a dense \((n_c+n_z)\times(n_x+n_u)\) block, filled by central differences (for M-01: 60 × 13 × 11 = 8580 entries, the inequality count IPOPT reports);
  • waypoint rows: two analytic entries each.

The tests compare the whole Jacobian with a dense finite-difference one.

Hessian. Second derivatives are not computed. IPOPT approximates the Hessian of the Lagrangian with a limited-memory BFGS update (section 8.2).

docs.title: 8. Using IPOPT
docs.text: IPOPT (Interior Point OPTimizer) is the open-source solver that computes every optimum in this repository. This chapter explains what it does, how the code hands it the problem, what every option does, how to read its log, and what to do when a solve fails. Installation is covered in chapter 1.

docs.title: 8.1 The problem IPOPT solves
docs.text:
IPOPT solves smooth nonlinear programs of the form

\[ \min_{y\in\mathbb R^n} f(y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_L \le g(y) \le g_U,\qquad y_L \le y \le y_U , \]

where \(f\) and \(g\) are twice continuously differentiable. Equality constraints have \(g_L = g_U\); one-sided inequalities have an infinite bound. The collocated trajectory problem of chapter 7 has exactly this form: \(y\) is the scaled decision vector, \(f\) the cost, and \(g\) stacks the defects and boundary rows (\(g_L = g_U = 0\)) and the path and waypoint rows (\(g_L = -\infty\), \(g_U = 0\)).

IPOPT finds a local solution: a point that satisfies the first-order optimality (KKT) conditions. It does not guarantee the global optimum, which is why the initial point matters (chapter 6).

docs.title: 8.2 How IPOPT works
docs.text:
The method is described in Wächter and Biegler, On the implementation of an interior-point filter line-search algorithm for large-scale nonlinear programming, Mathematical Programming 106 (2006). The main ideas, in the order they act in each iteration:

Slacks and barrier. Inequalities are turned into equalities with slack variables, \(g(y) - s = 0\) with \(g_L\le s\le g_U\). The bounds on \(y\) and \(s\) are then replaced by logarithmic barrier terms, which tend to infinity at the bounds:

\[ \min_{y,s}\; \varphi_\mu(y,s) = f(y) - \mu\sum_i \ln(y_i - y_{L,i}) - \mu\sum_i \ln(y_{U,i} - y_i) - \mu\sum_j \ln(s_j - g_{L,j}) - \mu\sum_j\ln(g_{U,j} - s_j) \]

subject to \(g(y) - s = 0\) (terms with infinite bounds are omitted). For a fixed barrier parameter \(\mu>0\) the iterates stay strictly inside the bounds; as \(\mu\to0\), the solutions of the barrier problems approach the solution of the original problem.

Newton step. For the current \(\mu\), IPOPT applies Newton's method to the optimality conditions of the barrier problem. Each iteration solves one sparse, symmetric, indefinite linear system:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} W_k + \Sigma_k + \delta_w I & J_k^\top \\ J_k & -\delta_c I \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Delta y \\ \Delta\lambda \end{bmatrix} = -\begin{bmatrix} \nabla\varphi_\mu + J_k^\top\lambda_k \\ c(y_k) \end{bmatrix}, \]

where \(J_k\) is the constraint Jacobian, \(W_k\) the Hessian of the Lagrangian, \(\Sigma_k\) a diagonal matrix from the barrier terms and \(\lambda\) the constraint multipliers. The regularisations \(\delta_w\) and \(\delta_c\) are added only when the matrix has the wrong inertia (column lg(rg) of the log). Because each collocation interval couples only neighbouring nodes, this matrix is very sparse, and a sparse direct solver (MUMPS by default) factorises it at a cost that grows roughly linearly with the number of nodes.

Hessian approximation. The code does not provide second derivatives. IPOPT builds a limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) approximation of \(W_k\) from the last few changes of the gradient of the Lagrangian (lbfgs_history pairs, default 6). This needs more iterations than an exact Hessian, but each iteration is cheap and nothing beyond first derivatives has to be coded.

Filter line search. The step is accepted if it sufficiently reduces either the barrier objective or the constraint violation, compared with a "filter" of previously seen pairs. This avoids a penalty parameter to balance the two. If the step is rejected, the step length \(\alpha\) is halved (column ls counts the trials), possibly after a second-order correction that reduces the constraint violation.

Restoration phase. If no acceptable step can be found, IPOPT temporarily ignores the objective and minimises the constraint violation, to return to a region where the filter accepts steps. Iterations in this phase are marked with r in the log. A solve that keeps entering restoration usually has a poor initial point or locally inconsistent constraints.

Barrier update. When the barrier problem is solved accurately enough, \(\mu\) is reduced. With mu_strategy = monotone, \(\mu\) only decreases, by a fixed rule. With adaptive (the default in this code), \(\mu\) is recomputed every iteration from the current complementarity, and may also increase temporarily.

Termination. IPOPT stops with Optimal Solution Found when the scaled optimality error (the largest of dual infeasibility, constraint violation and complementarity) is below tol, and the unscaled constraint violation is below constr_viol_tol (plus absolute tests on dual infeasibility and complementarity, left at IPOPT's defaults). It stops with Solved To Acceptable Level if the looser acceptable_tol is met for 15 consecutive iterations without reaching tol. Otherwise it stops at max_iter, max_cpu_time_s, or on an error.

docs.title: 8.3 How the code calls IPOPT
docs.text:
The solver interface is src/solver/ipopt_solver.cpp. It is the only file that includes IPOPT headers. Its Adapter class implements IPOPT's C++ interface Ipopt::TNLP for any nlp::Problem (nlp.hpp):

IPOPT callback What the adapter returns From nlp::Problem get_nlp_info Number of variables and constraints, number of Jacobian nonzeros, no Hessian numVariables, numConstraints, structure of constraintJacobian get_bounds_info Scaled variable bounds \(y_{L,U} = z_{L,U}/s\); constraint bounds variableBounds, constraintBounds get_starting_point Scaled initial point \(y_0 = z_0/s\) initialPoint eval_f Cost at \(z = s\,y\) cost eval_grad_f Gradient with respect to \(y\): \(\partial f/\partial y_j = s_j\,\partial f/\partial z_j\) costGradient eval_g Constraint values constraints eval_jac_g First call: row and column of every nonzero. Later calls: values, scaled by the column's variable scale constraintJacobian eval_h Not implemented: limited-memory Hessian intermediate_callback Records the iteration count finalize_solution Stores the final point (unscaled), the objective and the status

Four details matter in practice:

  1. Scaling. IPOPT sees \(y = z/s\), with the scales of section 7.10, so every variable it handles is of order one. IPOPT's own gradient-based scaling (nlp_scaling_method, on by default) still applies on top.
  2. Fixed sparsity. The Jacobian structure is recorded once, from the initial point, and every later evaluation must return the same entries in the same order. CollocationProblem guarantees this; a custom problem must too.
  3. Robustness. If an evaluation produces a non-finite number (for example a square root of a negative number far from the solution), the callback returns false. IPOPT then shortens the step instead of failing.
  4. Options. The adapter always sets hessian_approximation = limited-memory and suppresses IPOPT's banner (sb = yes). The other options come from the solver block of the case file (section 8.5).

Without IPOPT, the same file compiles a stub whose nlp::solve returns the status no_solver immediately, so the rest of the library builds and runs.

docs.title: The header
docs.text: The problem sizes match section 7.9: 661 variables (\(1 + 11\times60\)), 484 equalities (8 × 59 defects + 12 boundary rows) and 780 inequalities (13 rows × 60 nodes). The 421 bounded variables are \(t_f\) and the seven bounded states and controls at each node (\(1 + 7\times60\)). The 8580 inequality nonzeros are the dense 13 × 11 path blocks of the 60 nodes. "Number of nonzeros in Lagrangian Hessian: 0" confirms the limited-memory approximation.

docs.title: The iteration columns
docs.text: Column Meaning iter Iteration number. A trailing r marks the restoration phase objective Cost \(f\) at the current point (here: the normalised fuel plus the smoothness penalty) inf_pr Primal infeasibility: largest constraint violation of the internal (scaled, slack) problem inf_du Dual infeasibility: size of the gradient of the Lagrangian, which is zero at an optimum lg(mu) \(\log_{10}\) of the barrier parameter ‖d‖ Size of the step (largest component) lg(rg) \(\log_{10}\) of the Hessian regularisation \(\delta_w\); - when none was needed alpha_du, alpha_pr Step lengths of the multipliers and of the variables; 1 is a full Newton step letter after alpha_pr Type of step: f reduces the objective, h reduces the infeasibility, F/H the same with a second-order correction, R start of restoration, w watchdog, s soft restoration, t/T tiny step ls Number of line-search trials

docs.title: What this log shows
docs.text:
• Iterations 0–9. The warm start violates the collocation equations by 0.3 (largest scaled defect). With \(\mu\) still large, IPOPT reduces the violation to 0.004 and lets the cost rise from 0.46 to 1.56 on the way.
  • Iterations 10–42. The adaptive barrier update drops \(\mu\), not monotonically, to its floor of \(10^{-11}\). The cost falls to 0.390, its final value to three digits.
  • Iterations 42–100. IPOPT refines the solution at the smallest \(\mu\). Several H steps (second-order corrections) and two short steps at iterations 59–60 (alpha_pr 0.09 and 0.03, 3 and 4 line-search trials) show the line search working around curvature that the L-BFGS approximation captures imperfectly.
  • End. Dual infeasibility \(9.3\cdot10^{-7}\) and constraint violation \(4.4\cdot10^{-9}\) are below tol = \(10^{-6}\) and constr_viol_tol = \(10^{-6}\). The scaled and unscaled values coincide because IPOPT's own gradient scaling did not need to act on this already scaled problem.
  • Cost of evaluations. 129 cost and constraint evaluations for 101 Jacobians: the line search rarely needed extra trials.

EXIT: Optimal Solution Found. corresponds to solved; EXIT: Solved To Acceptable Level. to acceptable.

docs.title: 8.5 Options reference
docs.text:
All options go in the solver block of the pipeline object (section 3.4). They are passed to IPOPT under the names in the third column; the IPOPT documentation describes them in full.

Case-file key Default here IPOPT option (IPOPT's own default) When to change it tol \(10^{-6}\) tol (\(10^{-8}\)) Smaller for very accurate optima; larger (10⁻⁵) for faster, rougher studies. Very small values may be hard to reach, because the path Jacobian is computed by finite differences acceptable_tol \(10^{-4}\) acceptable_tol (\(10^{-6}\)) Smaller to forbid early acceptable stops; the verification still checks the result with verify_tol constr_viol_tol \(10^{-6}\) constr_viol_tol (\(10^{-4}\)) Rows are normalised, so \(10^{-6}\) means one part per million of each limit max_iter 1500 max_iter (3000) Raise if a slow but steady solve hits the limit; lower to fail fast in batch studies max_cpu_time_s 120 max_cpu_time (\(10^{20}\)) Per stage, in seconds. Raise for long missions with many nodes print_level 0 print_level (5) 5 for the iteration log; up to 12 for internal detail (very verbose) mu_strategy adaptive mu_strategy (monotone) Try monotone if the adaptive update oscillates or a solve stalls with \(\mu\) jumping up and down lbfgs_history 6 limited_memory_max_history (6) Larger values (10–20) can reduce the iteration count at a higher cost per iteration; worth testing on slow FC stages linear_solver IPOPT's default linear_solver (mumps in most builds) ma27, ma57, ma86 or ma97 if your IPOPT is linked with the HSL library: often faster on large problems derivative_test false derivative_test = first-order (none) When you change a model or add a constraint (section 8.6)

Options not in this table are not exposed by the case file. To set others (for example bound_push, nlp_scaling_method or max_wall_time), add one line to nlp::solve in ipopt_solver.cpp, next to the existing SetNumericValue and SetStringValue calls.

docs.title: 8.6 Checking derivatives
docs.text:
"derivative_test": true makes IPOPT compare the gradient and the Jacobian provided by the code with its own forward finite differences at the initial point, before the first iteration. Entries whose relative difference exceeds \(10^{-4}\) are printed:

Starting derivative checker for first derivatives.

* jac_g [    0,    5] = -1.5296645151557546e-04 v  ~ -1.5298873279334657e-04  [ 1.456e-04]
* jac_g [    8,   13] =  7.2836162465619590e-05 v  ~  7.2741812573440257e-05  [ 9.435e-04]
...
Derivative checker detected 14 error(s).

Each line gives the constraint row and the variable column, the value from the code, IPOPT's finite-difference estimate, and the relative difference. The run above (UF stage of M-01 with 12 nodes) flags 14 entries, all of order \(10^{-4}\) with relative differences between \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-3}\). That is the noise of a one-sided finite difference, not an error: the unit tests confirm the same Jacobian against central differences to about \(10^{-10}\). A real derivative error shows up differently, as relative differences of order one, often along a whole row or column. Use the checker on a small problem (few nodes), because it costs one constraint evaluation per variable.

docs.title: 8.7 When a solve fails
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause What to try infeasible from the first stage The mission is contradictory: start or goal within a zone's margin, a waypoint that cannot be reached with the turn radius, a climb steeper than the envelope allows over the distance Check the geometry (section 3.7); plot the warm start with --optimal infeasible or many r iterations with a cold start The straight-line seed crosses the zones Use "seed": "warm" max_iter with slowly decreasing inf_du Badly resolved trajectory or a flat optimum More nodes; or accept a looser tol; or raise max_iter max_iter with lg(mu) jumping up and down Adaptive barrier update oscillating "mu_strategy": "monotone" acceptable instead of solved Progress stalls near the tolerance, usually from finite-difference noise in the path Jacobian Normally harmless: the verification checks the result. Raise tol to \(10^{-5}\) if you prefer solved failed with Restoration_Failed Locally inconsistent constraints, often at the very start Check the boundary conditions: V_mps within the envelope, h0_m above h_min_m failed with Invalid_Number_Detected An evaluation returned NaN or infinity at the initial point Check the aircraft data; the initial point is evaluated before any step can be shortened Stage solved! (verification failed) IPOPT's scaled convergence test passed, but a row exceeds verify_tol in the original scaling Tighten constr_viol_tol; read the worst row in the summary line FC fails while UF succeeds Seed far from the 6-DoF optimum, or a 6-DoF limit (incidence, sideslip, rates) that the point mass ignores Check the worst row; increase nodes_fc; try "fc_from_uf": false to seed with the FC autopilot run

Chapter 10 lists failures outside the solver (build, input, planner).

docs.title: 8.8 Using IPOPT for your own problem
docs.text:
Any problem that implements the nlp::Problem interface can be solved with nlp::solve and checked with nlp::verify, with the same options and status reporting. Chapter 11 shows the interface and an example.

docs.title: 9. Example catalogue
docs.text:
The repository ships ten case files in code/data/cases/. This chapter describes each one: what it demonstrates, which inputs matter, what to look at in the output, and where its results are discussed. The examples are listed in the order in which they build on each other, from the aircraft to the optimiser.

All examples use the generic UAV of data/aircraft/generic_uav.json: 11 kg, 2.9 m span, 800 W, cruise speed 25 m/s. Its mass, geometry, inertia and stability derivatives follow the Aerosonde-class model of Beard and McLain (2012); its drag polar, propulsion and envelope limits are illustrative values.

docs.title: UC-01: aircraft report
docs.text:
File. uc01_aircraft_report.json. Key input: altitudes_m.

Prints the aircraft data and the quantities derived from it: maximum lift coefficient, induced-drag factor, maximum lift-to-drag ratio, and for each altitude the density, stall speed, best lift-to-drag speed, available power and thrust at cruise speed.

What to look at. This is the first case to run with a new aircraft. The stall speed and the best lift-to-drag speed bracket the speeds a minimum-fuel optimum will fly (20.8 m/s at sea level for the generic UAV, which is where the UC-08 and tutorial optima settle). The minimum turn radius at cruise speed and maximum bank (76 m) tells you how tight the missions can be.

docs.title: UC-02: trim
docs.text:
File. uc02_trim.json. Key input: flight (speed, altitude, flight-path angle, bank).

Trims the point-mass model in closed form and the rigid-body model by Newton iterations on the force and moment balance.

What to look at. Both models need the same thrust (9.27 N against 9.25 N at 25 m/s), because they share the lift and drag description. The 6-DoF trim (incidence 3.2°, elevator -8.1°) is the initial state of every FC stage (section 7.6). If the 6-DoF trim fails to converge for your aircraft, the FC stage cannot start.

docs.title: UC-03: open-loop simulation
docs.text:
File. uc03_simulation.json. Key inputs: duration_s, dt_s, uf.bank_cmd_deg, fc.elevator_doublet_deg.

Integrates both models with RK4: the point mass rolls into a 30° coordinated turn; the rigid body starts from trim and receives an elevator doublet.

What to look at. The point-mass turn rate matches \(g\tan\phi/V\) at constant altitude. The 6-DoF response shows the two longitudinal modes: the short period (a fast incidence oscillation that dies out in about 1 s) and the phugoid (a slow exchange of speed and altitude with a period of about 12 s). A new aircraft whose doublet response diverges is unstable, and its 6-DoF optimisation will be hard.

docs.title: UC-04: transcription check
docs.text:
File. uc04_transcription.json. Key inputs: mission (a straight 3.1 km leg with a 100 m climb), N (list of node counts).

Builds the point-mass collocation problem for several node counts and reports its size, its sparsity, the defects of a cold start and of a trimmed straight line, and the time to compute the defect Jacobian analytically and by finite differences.

What to look at. This example makes chapter 7 concrete. The number of variables is \(1+11N\); only 0.44 % of the Jacobian entries are nonzero at \(N=200\); the analytic Jacobian agrees with finite differences to about \(10^{-10}\) and is 57 to 487 times faster, because finite differences cost one full evaluation per variable. A cold start violates the dynamics by order one, a trimmed line not at all: the reason for the warm start (section 6.1).

docs.title: UC-05: design charts
docs.text:
File. uc05_design_charts.json. Key inputs: altitudes_m, trim_altitude_m, turn_speeds_mps.

Computes power curves, the flight envelope with ceilings, 6-DoF trim curves against speed, and level-turn performance.

What to look at. The envelope (stall speed to maximum level speed, 15.1 to 36.9 m/s at sea level) bounds what the optimiser can do; the minimum-time tutorial optimum flies at 39 m/s only because it dives. The trim curves show that elevator authority, not stall, sets the minimum trimmed speed of this aircraft. Run this case for every new aircraft: unrealistic coefficients show up here as unreachable trim or odd power curves.

docs.title: UC-06: typical design scenarios
docs.text:
File. uc06_design_scenarios.json. Key inputs: scenarios (straight or 180° turn, level or +200 m climb), speed_sweep_mps, nodes.

Flies four manoeuvres with the guidance laws of the warm start, with both models, and sweeps the commanded speed to find the least-fuel speed.

What to look at. The two models agree to within 0.2–67 m and burn the same fuel. Climbs are power-limited. The least-fuel speed (22 m/s) sits next to the best lift-to-drag speed, which anticipates the minimum-fuel optima of UC-08. The defects of the flown trajectories on 60 and 240 nodes show that the mesh must resolve the fastest manoeuvre (section 6.10).

docs.title: UC-07: missions with no-fly zones and waypoints
docs.text:
File. uc07_nfz_missions.json. Key inputs: missions (same format as UC-08), planner, nodes.

Plans each mission with Hybrid A* and flies the path with both models. These are exactly the warm starts of UC-08.

Mission Content M-01 One zone on the direct route M-02 Slalom between two zones M-03 Two waypoints, no zone M-04 One zone, one waypoint, a 150 m climb and a final heading change; a low zone on the direct route is overflown

What to look at. The flown trajectories keep 11–16 m outside every margin and pass within about 1 m of each waypoint. The column nfzCold shows how far a straight-line cold start would intrude into the zones (200–394 m inside): the situation the warm start avoids. Use this case to check a new mission's geometry before optimising it: if the planner finds no path here, UC-08 will start from a straight line.

docs.title: UC-08: optimal missions
docs.text:
File. uc08_optimal_missions.json. Key inputs: the whole pipeline block and missions (chapter 3).

The four UC-07 missions, optimised for minimum fuel with the full pipeline: warm start, point-mass optimum on 60 nodes, projection, 6-DoF optimum on 60 nodes, verification.

What to look at. Every stage converges and passes the verification; the optimal paths keep 9–12 m beyond every margin between nodes; the two models agree to 0.5 % in time and 0.2 % in fuel. The optima slow to the best lift-to-drag speed, pass the waypoints on their tolerance circles, and shorten the planner's path by hugging the zone corners. Mission M-04 is the richest: it combines a zone, a waypoint, a climb and an overflown zone. Chapter 4 explains every output of this case, and Worked examples: UC-08 discusses the results with figures.

To adapt it. Copy it under a new name, replace the missions with yours, and keep the pipeline block (chapter 5 shows the procedure).

docs.title: UC-09: warm-start benchmark
docs.text:
File. uc09_warmstart_benchmark.json. Key inputs: pipelines, repeats, and the same pipeline and missions as UC-08.

Solves each mission with four pipelines: COLD>UF, WS>UF, WS>FC and WS>UF>FC. All pipelines solve identical problems, so their iterations, times and optima can be compared directly.

What to look at. With this small aircraft, the cold start still converges, but needs up to twice the iterations and in M-04 reaches a worse local optimum (+3.9 % cost). Seeding the FC stage with the UF optimum or with the FC autopilot run leads to the same 6-DoF optimum. This is the public counterpart of the thesis benchmark (14. Warm-start benchmark), where the cold start failed in 3 of 8 scenarios.

To adapt it. Put your own missions in it to measure, on your problem, whether the warm start and the UF stage pay off.

docs.title: Tutorial: first mission
docs.text:
File. tutorial_first_mission.json. Key inputs: three missions T-01 (empty airspace), T-02 (one zone), T-03 (zone, waypoint and 100 m climb).

The worked example of chapter 5, written with every pipeline setting explicit so that it can serve as a template. It is not run by run.sh; run it by hand and plot it with python utils/plot_results.py --optimal output/tutorial.

docs.text: Problems are grouped by the moment they appear: while building, while reading the input, during the warm start, during the optimisation, and when looking at the results. Solver failures are covered in more depth in section 8.7.

docs.title: 10.3 Warm start
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Remedy warm start: planner found no path after N expansions The zones (plus margin and safety_m) block every route at the planning turn radius, the start or goal is inside a zone, or a waypoint lies inside one Check the geometry with a plot; reduce safety_m; refine the grid (cell_m 10, heading_bins 144); increase bank_fraction for tighter planned turns; reduce V_mps or increase bank_deg warm start: guidance did not reach the end of the path The path has turns too tight for the guidance, or the time budget ran out Reduce bank_fraction so the guidance has bank in reserve; check that V_mps is a comfortable speed for the aircraft The warm start is slow (seconds) Large search space: long missions, fine grid, many zones Coarser grid (cell_m 30–40); it only needs to be good enough to seed the optimiser

When the warm start fails, the UF stage starts from a straight line and the row is marked (CHECK) even if the optimisation succeeds. The optimum may still be valid: check its status and clearances.

docs.title: 10.4 Optimisation
docs.text: Symptom Remedy UC-08 prints skipped: this build has no IPOPT Build with IPOPT (chapter 1) A stage ends infeasible, max_iter, max_time or failed See section 8.7 A stage converges but is marked ! The verification found a row or bound violated by more than verify_tol; its label is printed (section 4.3). Tighten constr_viol_tol, or look at the named row: it identifies the constraint that IPOPT's scaled convergence test did not enforce tightly enough The run is very slow Reduce the nodes, run "stages": "UF" only, or lower max_cpu_time_s to fail fast. With many missions, run several case files in parallel processes Different iteration counts from those in this documentation Expected: they depend on the IPOPT version and its linear solver. Optima agree to the printed digits

docs.title: 10.5 Results that look wrong
docs.text: Observation Explanation or remedy The optimum passes close to the zone, not in the middle of the gap Expected: the cost decides the path, and the margin is the only distance required. Increase margin_m for more distance The waypoint is passed exactly on its tolerance circle Expected for minimum fuel: going closer costs fuel. Reduce tolerance_m if you need to pass closer The airspeed falls sharply at the end The final speed is free; a minimum-fuel optimum keeps no kinetic energy it does not need. Add a final-speed condition in code if required (section 11.6) The optimum flies over a zone The zone's altitude band does not overlap the mission's altitudes, so it is inactive (drawn hatched in grey). Raise h_max_m if it should be avoided Thrust or bank oscillate from node to node The smoothness weights are too small. Use beta_control and beta_state of about 1 The 6-DoF optimum burns noticeably less fuel than the point mass The sideslip limit was relaxed; the 6-DoF model is using side force as free lift. Keep sideslip_max_deg at 1 (section 7.4) clr is much larger than expected Few nodes: the zone margin is inflated by half the node spacing (section 7.5). More nodes reduce the inflation simUF of several metres Too few nodes for the manoeuvres; increase nodes_uf A cold start gives a different optimum from a warm start Both are local optima of the same problem; the lower cost is the better one. The warm start usually finds it

docs.title: 11. Using and extending the library
docs.text: Everything the ofc program does is available as a C++ library, ofc_core. This chapter shows how to link it, how to run the pipeline or a single optimisation stage from your own code, how to hand IPOPT a problem of your own, and how to add new constraints.

docs.title: 11.1 The library
docs.text:
ofc_core is a static library built from every source in code/src/ except main.cpp. Its public headers are in code/include/ofc/, one per module; Architecture shows how they depend on each other.

Namespace Header Content ofc aircraft.hpp, mission.hpp, types.hpp Aircraft (loading, validation, derived performance), MissionSpec, vectors and rotations ofc::isa atmosphere.hpp Standard atmosphere ofc::uf, ofc::fc point_mass.hpp, rigid_body.hpp The two models: rhs, uf::jacobian, air data, coefficients ofc::trim, ofc::num, ofc::perf trim.hpp, numerics.hpp, performance.hpp Trim, RK4 and Newton, point performance ofc::env, ofc::plan environment.hpp, planner.hpp No-fly zones and waypoints, Dubins paths and Hybrid A* ofc::scenario, ofc::ws scenario.hpp, warm_start.hpp Guidance laws, warm start, cold starts, UF → FC projection ofc::ocp collocation.hpp, ocp_problem.hpp, ocp_uf.hpp, ocp_fc.hpp Decision-vector layout, collocation, the two optimal-control problems ofc::nlp nlp.hpp, solver.hpp The Problem interface, verify, solve (IPOPT) and its options ofc::pipeline pipeline.hpp run: the staged optimisation of one mission, and the post-checks ofc::io io.hpp JSON input, CSV and JSON output

docs.title: 11.2 Linking it from your project
docs.text:
The simplest way is to add the code/ folder as a CMake subdirectory:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.14)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

set(OFC_BUILD_TESTS OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)        # the library's tests are not needed here
add_subdirectory(path/to/uavtraj-opt/code ofc)

add_executable(my_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE ofc_core)       # headers, C++17 and IPOPT come with it

IPOPT is found exactly as in chapter 1, and OFC_IPOPT=ON can be set before add_subdirectory to make it mandatory. On Windows with the prebuilt IPOPT, the IPOPT DLLs must be next to your executable or on PATH; for example:

file(GLOB IPOPT_DLLS "$ENV{IPOPT_DIR}/bin/*.dll")
add_custom_command(TARGET my_app POST_BUILD
                   COMMAND ${CMAKE_COMMAND} -E copy_if_different ${IPOPT_DLLS} $<TARGET_FILE_DIR:my_app>)

The examples below load data/aircraft/generic_uav.json and data/cases/tutorial_first_mission.json with relative paths, so run them from code/. Both were compiled and run against the repository as described here; their output is shown after each listing.

docs.title: 11.3 Running the pipeline from C++
docs.text:
#include <cstdio>

#include "ofc/aircraft.hpp"
#include "ofc/io.hpp"
#include "ofc/mission.hpp"
#include "ofc/pipeline.hpp"

using namespace ofc;

int main() {
    const Aircraft ac = Aircraft::fromFile("data/aircraft/generic_uav.json");
    const nlohmann::json c = io::readJson("data/cases/tutorial_first_mission.json");
    const MissionSpec m = MissionSpec::fromJson(c.at("missions").at(1), ac); // T-02

    pipeline::Config cfg = pipeline::Config::fromJson(c.at("pipeline"));
    cfg.alpha = 0.0; // minimum time instead of minimum fuel

    const pipeline::Result r = pipeline::run(ac, m, cfg);
    std::printf("UF %s in %d iterations: t_f = %.1f s\n", r.uf.status.c_str(), r.uf.iterations, r.ufOpt.tf);
    std::printf("FC %s in %d iterations: t_f = %.1f s\n", r.fc.status.c_str(), r.fc.iterations, r.fcOpt.tf);
    std::printf("FC verification: %s\n", r.fc.check.summary().c_str());
    return r.ok() ? 0 : 1;
}

UF solved in 36 iterations: t_f = 90.4 s
FC acceptable in 78 iterations: t_f = 90.0 s
FC verification: dynamics ok | boundary ok | envelope ok | environment ok | bounds ok

pipeline::Config holds every setting of the pipeline block (section 3.4) as a C++ member: seed, uf, fc, fcFromUf, nodesUf, nodesFc, alpha, betaControl, betaState, sideslipMax, warmStart, solver, verifyTol. A default-constructed Config is the default pipeline (WS>UF>FC, minimum fuel, 60 nodes). Config::withLabel("WS>UF") returns a copy with another seed and stage sequence.

pipeline::Result contains the warm start (warm), the initial points and optima of both stages (ufGuess, ufOpt, fcGuess, fcOpt, each an ocp::Trajectory with tf, X and U), and the stage records (warmStage, uf, fc) with status, iterations, time, objective, seed and verification. pipeline::clearanceAlong, waypointMissAlong and ufSimulationError compute the post-checks of section 6.8.

docs.title: 11.4 Solving one stage by hand
docs.text:
To control each step yourself, build the problem from an initial point and call the solver directly:

#include <cstdio>

#include "ofc/aircraft.hpp"
#include "ofc/io.hpp"
#include "ofc/mission.hpp"
#include "ofc/ocp_uf.hpp"
#include "ofc/point_mass.hpp"
#include "ofc/solver.hpp"
#include "ofc/warm_start.hpp"

using namespace ofc;

int main() {
    const Aircraft ac = Aircraft::fromFile("data/aircraft/generic_uav.json");
    const nlohmann::json c = io::readJson("data/cases/tutorial_first_mission.json");
    const MissionSpec m = MissionSpec::fromJson(c.at("missions").at(1), ac); // T-02

    // 1. Initial point: the warm start, resampled on 40 nodes.
    const ws::Result warm = ws::build(ac, m, ws::Config{});
    if (!warm.ok) return 1;
    const ocp::Trajectory guess = ws::fromRun(warm.uf, 40);

    // 2. Problem: minimum fuel, standard smoothing, references from the mission.
    const Mission ms = m.ufMission(/*alpha=*/1.0, /*betaControl=*/1.0, /*betaState=*/1.0);
    const ocp::Reference ref{m.referenceLength(), m.referenceLength() / m.flight.V};
    const auto wps = ocp::assignWaypoints(guess, m.waypoints, uf::X, uf::Y);
    const ocp::UfProblem problem(ac, ms, guess, wps, ref);

    // 3. Solve and verify.
    nlp::Options opt;
    opt.printLevel = 0;
    const nlp::Result r = nlp::solve(problem, opt);
    const nlp::Verification v = nlp::verify(problem, r.z);
    const ocp::Trajectory t = problem.trajectory(r.z);
    std::printf("%s (%s), %d iterations, t_f = %.1f s, fuel = %.2f g\n", nlp::toString(r.status), r.message.c_str(),
                r.iterations, t.tf, 1e3 * (t.X.front()[uf::MASS] - t.X.back()[uf::MASS]));
    std::printf("%s\n", v.summary().c_str());
    return r.ok() && v.ok() ? 0 : 1;
}

solved (Solve_Succeeded), 63 iterations, t_f = 157.3 s, fuel = 6.44 g
dynamics ok | boundary ok | envelope ok | environment ok | bounds ok

Two differences from pipeline::run are worth knowing:

  • The zone margins are used as given. The pipeline inflates them so that the segments between nodes keep the margin (section 7.5); without it, only the nodes are guaranteed to. Inflate ms.nfz[j].margin yourself if you need the same guarantee.
  • Any ocp::Trajectory with the right number of states and controls can be the initial point: ws::coldUf for a straight line, a trajectory from a previous solve (resampled with ocp::resample), or your own.

ocp::FcProblem is used in the same way, with an ocp::FcMission (start state from ws::fcStartState, goal, heading, weights, sideslip limit, zones and altitude band) and a 6-DoF initial point, for example ws::ufToFc(ac, ocp::resample(ufOptimum, N)).

docs.title: 11.5 Your own problem with IPOPT
docs.text:
nlp::solve accepts any class derived from nlp::Problem (nlp.hpp):

Method Must return numVariables(), numConstraints() Problem size variableBounds(zl, zu), constraintBounds(gl, gu) Bounds; use ±nlp::kInf for "no bound" initialPoint() The starting point variableScale() (optional) Typical magnitude of each variable; default 1 cost(z), costGradient(z) Objective and its exact gradient constraints(z) Constraint values constraintJacobian(z) Nonzero entries as {row, col, value} triplets, with the same rows and columns in the same order at every call constraintLabel(i), constraintKind(i), variableLabel(j) (optional) Names and groups used by nlp::verify

A minimal example, the Rosenbrock function constrained to a disc:

#include <cstdio>

#include "ofc/nlp.hpp"
#include "ofc/solver.hpp"

using namespace ofc;

// min (1 - x)^2 + 100 (y - x^2)^2   subject to   x^2 + y^2 <= 1.5
class Rosenbrock : public nlp::Problem {
public:
    int numVariables() const override { return 2; }
    int numConstraints() const override { return 1; }
    void variableBounds(Vec& zl, Vec& zu) const override { zl = {-nlp::kInf, -nlp::kInf}, zu = {nlp::kInf, nlp::kInf}; }
    void constraintBounds(Vec& gl, Vec& gu) const override { gl = {-nlp::kInf}, gu = {1.5}; }
    Vec initialPoint() const override { return {-1.0, 1.0}; }
    double cost(const Vec& z) const override {
        return (1 - z[0]) * (1 - z[0]) + 100 * (z[1] - z[0] * z[0]) * (z[1] - z[0] * z[0]);
    }
    Vec costGradient(const Vec& z) const override {
        const double r = z[1] - z[0] * z[0];
        return {-2 * (1 - z[0]) - 400 * z[0] * r, 200 * r};
    }
    Vec constraints(const Vec& z) const override { return {z[0] * z[0] + z[1] * z[1]}; }
    std::vector<Triplet> constraintJacobian(const Vec& z) const override { return {{0, 0, 2 * z[0]}, {0, 1, 2 * z[1]}}; }
};

int main() {
    const Rosenbrock p;
    const nlp::Result r = nlp::solve(p);
    std::printf("%s: x = %.4f, y = %.4f\n", nlp::toString(r.status), r.z[0], r.z[1]);
    return r.ok() ? 0 : 1;
}

solved: x = 0.9072, y = 0.8228

The adapter of section 8.3 then applies the scaling, the limited-memory Hessian and the status mapping to your problem as it does to the trajectory problems.

docs.title: A new kind of environment constraint
docs.text:
Zones and waypoints of the existing kinds need no code: list them in the case file. A new kind (a circular zone, a ceiling, terrain clearance, a speed limit inside an area) touches six places:

  1. Model. Add a struct, a ...FromJson parser and a smooth, distance-like function to environment.hpp and environment.cpp.
  2. Mission data. Add a vector of it to MissionSpec (mission.hpp) and parse it in MissionSpec::fromJson.
  3. NLP rows. Add a member to Mission (transcription.hpp) and FcMission (ocp_fc.hpp). In both models, append one name to the path-row names and one value to pathAt, in the same order (TrapezoidalUF::pathConstraintNames and TrapezoidalUF::pathAt; the FcProblem constructor and FcProblem::pathAt). Write the row as \(h\le0\) and normalise it by a characteristic size. The Jacobian picks the new row up automatically (central differences per node). nlp::verify reports it in the environment group if its name starts with nfz:; extend CollocationProblem::constraintKind for other prefixes.
  4. Planner. If the constraint restricts the horizontal path, extend the free-space test in plan::planMission (planner.cpp), or the warm start will cross it.
  5. Pipeline. Pass the new data from MissionSpec to both problems in pipeline::run.
  6. Tests. Check the sign convention, a point inside and one outside, and a complete pipeline run that respects the constraint (tests/test_optimization.cpp).

The row must be smooth in the state: avoid switching it on and off with altitude or time inside pathAt (section 7.5 explains why zones are activated once per mission).

docs.title: A new boundary condition
docs.text:
Equality conditions at the start or the end (a final airspeed, a final flight-path angle) are boundary rows, added in the constructors of UfProblem (ocp_uf.cpp) and FcProblem. Each row is a label, a column of the decision vector, a target and a scale. For example, to impose a final airspeed in the UF problem, after the existing final-heading row:

// Final airspeed (m.speedEnd: a new member of Mission, filled from the case file).
if (m.speedEnd > 0.0) boundary.push_back({"xf.V", L.idxState(K, V), m.speedEnd, s.x[V]});

CollocationProblem adapts the constraint count, the Jacobian (one constant entry per boundary row) and the labels by itself. Add the corresponding row to FcProblem with the forward body velocity u if the FC stage must respect it too.

docs.title: 11.7 Tests and formatting
docs.text:
The unit tests in code/tests/ use no external framework: each file registers checks that tests/main.cpp runs. Add a test for every new model term, constraint or derivative, and compare any analytic derivative with nlp::jacobianError or a central difference. Run them with ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure -C Release, and format the sources with clang-format 18 before committing (section 1.7).
